hints: Remember what an ideal gas pretends, particles with no volume and no attractions between them at all.
Compare the four gases for size and strength of intermolecular forces, especially polarity and hydrogen bonding.
Pick the smallest, non-polar, monatomic gas with the weakest London forces, as it is hardest to liquefy and closest to those ideal assumptions.
walkthrough:
**Recall the ideal gas assumptions**

Think like an ideal particle. It has negligible volume and zero intermolecular forces.

Real gases deviate most when particles are large or attract each other strongly:
$$pV = nRT \text{ (ideal, no attractions, no volume)}$$

**Rank the gases by size and attractions**

Helium, $\text{He}$, is tiny, monatomic and non-polar with only extremely weak London forces.

Nitrogen, $\text{N}_2$, is larger and diatomic, krypton, $\text{Kr}$, is a large atom with many electrons and stronger London forces, while ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, is polar and hydrogen bonded.

**Choose the most ideal gas**

The smaller and less sticky the particles, the closer to ideal at room temperature and pressure.

Helium has the weakest attractions and smallest volume, so it deviates least and behaves most ideally.

options.A: Helium is correct. As a very small, monatomic, non-polar noble gas, $\text{He}$ has negligible particle volume and only extremely weak London dispersion forces, so it best matches the ideal assumptions of no volume and no attractions.
options.B: Nitrogen is not the best. $\text{N}_2$ is non-polar but it is diatomic and larger than helium with stronger London forces, so it deviates more from ideal behaviour.
options.C: Ammonia is the least ideal. $\text{NH}_3$ is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, which are strong intermolecular attractions. This causes a large deviation from the no-attraction assumption.
options.D: Krypton is not ideal. $\text{Kr}$ is a large noble gas atom with many electrons, so it has relatively strong London forces and is much more easily liquefied than helium.
